newsitem.title: USA: Conn. governor seeks tax cuts in FY98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Conn. governor seeks tax cuts in FY98 budget.

text.p: Connecticut Governor John Rowland on Thursday proposed cutting the income tax by one third for most state residents, shaving the gasoline tax by five cents per gallon and trimming the state's work force.
The Republican Rowland in his fiscal year 1998 budget speech also recommended $37 million in initiatives called for by the state's school desegregation task force.
Rowland proposed an early retirement incentive plan that he said could save the state $100 million annually in personnel costs.
But state Demomcrats quickly said they had some serious problems with the budget.
"It reminds me of the problem of looking in rear view mirrors -- sometimes things seem larger than they really are," said Sen. Kevin D. Sullivan, a Democrat, the top-ranking official in the Senate.

"It's good news that the governor's bottom line is very low, (but) it's also clear that the level of spending proposed in this budget is in fact higher than the level of spending adopted by the legislature a year ago," Sullivan told Reuters.

"It is lower than this year's actual expenditures, but that's in part because the governor uses this budget proposal to front-load some of next year's costs into this year's budget in order to make a better comparison."
Sullivan said the Democrats shared Rowland's goal of a "low growth or no growth" budget, as well as that of a major tax cut for most residents.

"There are so-called cuts in this budget which are very large and very much speculative and unspecified, including an early retirement option that is supposed to save $100 million plus," Sullivan said.
"The only other two times Connecticut has done this, we have actually lost money... So one has to be a little skeptical."

"I think you'll see a debate over priorities. We are very much troubled that the commitment to education -- while there are some good signs on early childhood -- overall, it is a budget which cuts funding to education in the state. That can't be good news for our economy."
Sullivan said most of Rowland's proposed gas tax cut would be paid for "by eliminating a tax break for local property tax payers on motor vehicles, which is scheduled to go into effect next year."
The gas tax cut would also be financed by increased charges for bus and rail use, and by a hike in the diesel fuel tax, Sullivan said.
"So in large measure, it just trades one tax for another. I don't think that's what people had in mind."
The Democrats target the same spending bottom line as Rowland, Sullivan said.

"What we're going to say is, 'Governor, come back and work with us, because we cannot do this to children and education in the future in the state of Connecticut. We're going to have to find cuts elsewhere."

Democrats "want to cut taxes in a way that gives the greatest relief to the people with the highest tax burdens," Sullivan said. "That is a combination of income tax reduction, and targetting it in some fashion to people paying high property taxes."
